A1.notes.Q3: Course credits and grades matter for planning my own studies, but page views (Absalon) feel like surveillance on how students spend their lives outside class time.
A1.notes.Q4: If I can't explain why a student was flagged, my trust in the outreach collapses completely. Advisors need clear reasons to intervene effectively.
A1.notes.Q5: Equity is crucial so we don't miss students from underrepresented backgrounds, but a slightly lower overall rate of help is better than missing specific groups.
A1.notes.Q6: Students often don't ask for what they need until it's too late; I want to be there early, regardless of the specific trigger.
A1.notes.Q7: A personalized message requires careful handling; false positives damage the advisor-student relationship more than missed opportunities do.

A2.notes.Q3: I feel course grades are vital for early warning, but high-school GPA feels outdated and irrelevant to current struggles. Online activity (page views) seems intrusive; I'd need a large accuracy gain before accepting it as surveillance. Sensitive data like age or disability status shouldn't be needed—I prefer existing criteria that flag anyone struggling regardless of background.
A2.notes.Q4: My students need to understand exactly why they are being flagged so we can trust the process and fix the specific issue (e.g., missed deadline) rather than generic support. 'Very high' explainability is non-negotiable for my role, even if it misses a few cases.
A2.notes.Q5: We can't afford to systematically miss groups based on background or gender—it harms the student-adviseur relationship and perpetuates inequality. However, we also shouldn't just contact everyone (low precision) as that wastes advisors' time and overloads students.
A2.notes.Q6: I think the intervention depends on severity, but since we are identifying via model, a generic email is safer initially to reduce stigma, followed by personalized contact if needed.

A3.notes.Q3: Credit performance is crucial but grades alone aren't enough; need strong signal to avoid bias from school type (high school GPA). Disability and financial aid are sensitive contexts where small misses hurt, so higher thresholds seem right.
A3.notes.Q4: Trust is vital for outreach to work. Very low explainability makes students defensive; we'd need a huge gain in identification (around 5-10) to justify it, but that feels risky without clear reasons.
A3.notes.Q5: Fairness can't come at the cost of missing students in need overall. If we miss more from a group (e.g., women or low-income), it feels like discrimination even if contact rates are equal.
A3.notes.Q6: Students shouldn't wait to ask for help; we can spot early signs. Personalization builds trust better than generic emails, and continuous monitoring helps catch issues faster.
A3.notes.Q7: With personalized messages (advisors involved), the harm of false positives is higher so we need to be very selective. For generic emails, maybe reaching out slightly more broadly doesn't cause as much distress.
A3.Q8.1: I worry about how the university handles data when a flag comes back; there needs to be a human-in-the-loop review before any notification goes out, regardless of model confidence.

S1.notes.Q3: Grade data is okay if we catch many at risk, but admin/high-school GPA feels like judging my past life before I start here.
S1.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly what triggered the warning before I feel comfortable taking any action based on it.
S1.notes.Q5: My own struggles make fairness critical; missing anyone feels like a second chance lost, but catching everyone is too expensive.
S1.notes.Q6: As someone who dropped out twice, I want immediate help rather than waiting for a yearly check-in or an email.
S1.notes.Q7: A generic email is useless unless it's personalized to my specific situation and tone matches the support offered.

S2.notes.Q3: Course grades feel fair, but Absalon data feels like surveillance. Financial aid status is high risk since I work part-time to pay costs; bias here would be unfair.
S2.notes.Q4: I need a clear reason if I get flagged, otherwise it feels like an algorithmic punishment without recourse.
S2.notes.Q5: Missing students from my group (immigrants) is worse than false positives. It's about not being seen as equal at the start.
S2.notes.Q6: Too much contact feels intrusive and creates noise for students already doing fine; annual check-ins are enough without being spied on.
S2.notes.Q7: General emails can be low threshold, but personalized messages must only go to those who actually need help to avoid stigma.

S3.notes.Q3: Course grades make sense, but I fear 'Absalon data' (page views) is creepy and reveals habits beyond academics. For sensitive data, age helps contextually; disability needs proof anyway, so a moderate lift justifies it for me.
S3.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I was flagged because it affects my self-esteem and how advisors explain support plans. 'Very low' is out of the question for me personally.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness isn't just about accuracy; it's about not missing people from my specific situation who need help due to bias in past data.
S3.notes.Q6: If the system detects a problem, I want immediate support now, not just once a year or after symptoms worsen.
S3.notes.Q7: For generic emails, sending it out more often is fine (it's low stakes). For personalized advisor contact with my specific history, I'd prefer high precision to avoid unnecessary pressure.

S4.notes.Q3: Course grades are useful for me since I have failed before, but high-school GPA feels too far away from my current struggles with ADHD planning deadlines.
S4.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I was flagged because my diagnosis is ADHD; a vague algorithmic reason makes me defensive and unwilling to accept help.
S4.notes.Q5: We must catch every student in need, especially marginalized groups like first-gen students who might otherwise be invisible or unfairly penalized for non-academic reasons.
S4.notes.Q6: Given my history of dropping out, waiting until I fail a course is too late. Proactive and continuous contact is essential for early intervention.
S4.notes.Q7: For generic emails, it's okay to cast a wider net as the risk of false alarms is low. For personalized messages that name me or my specific issues, precision matters more.

S5.notes.Q3: Grades seem okay with large improvement needed since it feels like I've already paid for this data via my tuition and grades are visible to me as an instructor.
S5.notes.Q4: I'd accept less explanation if the model is significantly better at catching people I've seen struggle before, but right now trust in 'black box' algorithms for my own support needs to be high.
S5.notes.Q5: I think it's hard to balance being fair across everyone while helping me specifically if I'm from a minority group, so I'd take slightly less overall help than we miss people who are actually struggling.

S6.notes.Q3: Course performance is okay if it helps identify me specifically, since I struggle with deadlines and grades sometimes. Disability info must be small improvement because I need early intervention before falling behind completely.
S6.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I was flagged (e.g., late submissions) so my advisor can talk about it directly. Very low explainability feels like a black box judgment.
S6.notes.Q5: As an international student, I worry the model misses me because of language barriers or being first-gen. Missing struggling students hurts more than unnecessary contacts do for fair treatment.
S6.notes.Q6: A personalized email feels invasive without my consent, but a generic one is less risky. I want to avoid being contacted unnecessarily just because of patterns.
S6.notes.Q7: When I don't need help and get a generic email it's annoying when unnecessary contact is avoided.
S6.Q8.1: I feel like the university already notices me falling behind because of my history with dropping out, but early warning based on data could prevent that before I reach crisis point.

S8.notes.Q5: False positives cause unnecessary stress and anxiety for marginalized groups who are already vulnerable to stigma.
S8.notes.Q6: Early detection is crucial, but the intervention must be low-pressure; generic emails feel safer than a phone call.
S8.notes.Q7: A personalized email or meeting feels too intrusive for someone who might just need space, so selective outreach is better.

S9.notes.Q5: We shouldn't miss students in underrepresented groups even if it means flagging fewer people overall.
